Beastly "Majah" Alford.
Beastly "Majah" Alford.

Our readers all remember a colored barber and teacher of music who once flourished in Waco, who dubbed himself "Majah Alford, de only fuss-class musician in Waco, sah." "Majah," since giving up ton oral practice and musical pursuits and quitting Waco, has been teaching the young idea how to make night hideous by beating bass-drums and blowing villainous horns, in different parts of the state. It has already been announced to the public that Alford attempted to rape a fourteen-year-old girl of his class at Gainesville, and is now in custody and likely to remain so. Last Sunday it was fortunate for this beast that the guards at the jail could not be intimidated, or he might have been the principal actor at a necktie picnic. From the Gainesville Hesperian we get the following:

"On Sunday last a crowd numbering perhaps fifty or more went to the jail with the avowed intention of taking possession of the "Majah's" precious caress. Happily their demonstrations were confined to talk and theats, and a stand-off from the guards was taken quite submissively. We hope that the good, solid sense of the would-be avengers will show them that there are laws specially applicable to the case now at issue, and when the negro is given a fair trial, his crime, it any, will be speedily punished. To allow "lynch law" to have full scope in a city of our retensions would be a lasting disgrace and work incalculable injury to its prospects, although the crime committed is one of the most heinous known to man."

Alford has been teaching band music and dancing, and will no doubt if the charges against him be proven, do some dancing himself. He has always been a singular character, who feigned to know much more than he really did, and was far too forward with those he could in no wise approach in rank or station. Some years ago he made himself notorious among his race by constituting himself a democratic champion and challenging Gov. Davis to a joint controversy. "Majah" got too sharp to need any more sense or instruction, but had it to give grants to everyone else, and now in his old age he is about to learn a severe lesson.

Minnesota's claim under the five per cent. land bill is $39,203.57. Dunnell has already sent in the bill.

Some Minneapolis land speculators claim $5,000 damage from the Western Union Telegraph company for delaying the delivery of a message and spoiling a profitable deal.

Jack Riley, a cattle buyer, started from Lake Crystal on the 16th inst., with several hundred dollars in his possession and has not since been heard from. Fears are entertained that he has been foully dealt with.

Three tramps were given lodgings in Kohler's hotel in Shakopee, and during the night arose and gathered into themselves six boxes of cigars, plundered several of the inmates, and then like the Arabs of old, folded their tents and as silently stole away.

At Winnipeg last week poplar wood sold for $10, tamarac for $12 per cord. Hay commanded $25 per ton. Beef was sold at 25 cents per pound, and other meats in proportion, with a prospect of a still further rise if the then scarcity continued.

Special dispatch to Jacksonville Times.]
TAMPA FLORIDA March 6
A tramp (man) named Charles Owens, was hanged in a street of Tampa, between two and three o'clock P. M. to-day, by an outraged community for burglariously entering a house near town last night and assaulting, with intent to commit rape upon, one of our most respectable young ladies. He made a confession of his guilt before meeting his fate. JOHN P. WALL.

A correspondent of the Times, under date of March 7th, gives the following graphic account of the whole affair:

Yesterday at half-past two o'clock there occurred here one of the most awful tragedies that I ever witnessed, and the like of which has not occurred in the United States in the past twenty-four years. A prisoner, without trial, was taken from the jail, while the U. S. District Court was in session not ten steps away, carried across the street in front of the court-house and hanged to a shade tree. This occurred in open daylight, right in the centre of a town of over a thousand population.

THE CRIME.

The victim was a young white man about thirty years old, and of medium size and height, named C. D. Owens. His resemblance to Guiteau was remarkable. He came to this country from London about a year ago, and has been working at different little jobs, and making but a poor livelihood. On last Sunday afternoon he was seen in town rather the worse for liquor. Sunday night a person broke into the residence of one of our prominent citizens on Nebraska Avenue, and after committing several small thefts entered the sleeping apartment of a highly respectable young l
cape, leaving his victim in a fainting and almost dying condition. The neighbors were at once summoned and a search was promptly begun. THE PURSUIT. For fear of exciting the community, the matter was kept a profound secret and only the officers of the law and a few immediate friends knew anything about the case until the scoundrel was locked safely in jail. The sheriff and a posse
c-d-owens-tampa-1882-03-06.A2:
started in pursuit at about ten o'clock yesterday. They got a clew and followed it up and at twelve o'clock they overtook Owens beyond Krause's Spring, and after slight resistance captured him. Owens acknowledged to being in the house Sunday night, but said he only intended robbery. Afterwards he said he thought of rape, and then said he ought to have murdered the girl and hushed the matter up.

THE INFURIATED MOB.

He appeared to take the entire matter as a huge joke from the time he was arrested. In coming back to town, as he crossed the river, he threw a package overboard. He was placed in jail at about one o'clock. In the meantime the news of the intended rape had got wind and spread, and by the time the prisoner was safely behind the bars, the people had about determined to take the law in their own hands. In an hour's time an immense crowd had gathered, and a vote was called, and all who favored taking Owens out and hanging him to a tree were asked to step out. Nearly all stepped out. Then about twenty men volunteered to go up to the sheriff's home and get the jail keys. I am sure Mr. Craft did not think for a moment that the crowd intended harm. When the mob entered the sheriff's house, he was at his dinner. As he rose from the table a dozen pair of hands grabbed him, and before he knew what he was about, his keys were gone and the mob with them. The infuriated mob pressed on towards the jail. In the meantime the mob was growing larger every moment. The jail door was unlocked, and the prisoner was taken out. He was the most unconcerned and indifferent person present. He said: "Oh, you all can't bull-doze me. I will have a trial." Then he was hurried across the court-house yard, and then across the street under a large shade tree. A rope was passed over a limb, a noose made, and his hands were tied. Now, for the first time, the miserable wretch realized his fate. Before, he did not know what to think. I am sure he had no idea of being hung. As soon as he saw that the mob was in earnest, then he denied the crime and begged for his life. He said he would go to prison for life if only mercy were shown him. He begged for a trial, and the grimmest reply was given I ever heard: "Yes, we will give you a trial, but we will hang you first and try you afterwards."

THE LYNCHING.

Lieutenant Danes, of the Third Artillery, arrived on the ground, and as soon as he saw how matters stood he called the garrison to arms to rescue the prisoner. The sheriff had come down and the mayor of the town, and they were now all begging for the prisoner's life. The poor, friendless wretch saw that if he could only prolong his life a few minutes the troops in the garrison would rescue him. How he fought, how he begged for time, how he called on the crowd to help him! But in vain. The fair face of his intended victim was uppermost in the minds of the maddened throng. As soon as the teet and hands of the doomed man were tied a dray was driven under the tree and Owens placed thereon. When the dray moved off the rope slipped and the prisoner fell to the ground. The military were expected every moment, and now the mob must act quickly. So a half a dozen ready hands laid hold of the rope and drew the body of C. D. Owens up.

There the body hung in the public streets, out in front of the hall of justice, court sitting from day to day; there the body hung till sunset. The crowd slowly dispersed, the military did not come, and human vengeance was visited swiftly on this wretched man. May the God he has gone to meet have more mercy on him than did his fellowmen!

Tampa Tribune, March 16.]
Judge Locke vs. General Wall.
The action of any official is a legitimate rule.
Judge Locke vs. General Wall.

The action of any official is a legitimate subject of criticism, and probably none is more deserving of a critical review than that of a Judge when arbitrarily exercising the rights and powers with which he is invested as a court. On the second day of the Spring Term of the United States Court here last week, Judge Locke issued a rule against General J. B. Wall to show cause why he should not be stricken from the roll of attorneys practicing in his court for counselling and aiding in the unlawful hanging of a man in Tampa, on the 6th inst. General Wall very properly refused to put in an answer to such an accusation, but respectfully asked the court to waive the rule until after the Spring Term of the State court in this county, which would be holden this month. This Judge Locke refused to do, and last Friday issued an order disbarring General Wall until further order of the court.

In this act Judge Locke proceeded in a manner wholly at variance with the rulings of the Supreme Courts of the United States and of Florida, as was plainly demonstrated by Colonel Sparkman last Saturday in an argument before his court on a motion to vacate the order disbarring Mr. Wall, in not basing his rule on a sworn complaint, which both these courts have enunciated as necessary and requisite before the issue of the rule to show cause, &c. Instead of waiting for any such sworn complaint, Judge Locke issued the rule on hearsay, and a day or two subsequently called on the United States Marshal of his court to testify against General Wall; but even his evidence did not substantiate the facts alleged in the rule calling on General Wall to show cause, &c. This is a fair statement of the case and the law points involved, but we reserve our comments for another issue.

The Small-Pox Case.
This city was thrown into a level of excitement last Monday by the report that a genuine case of small-pox had developed itself in one of the negro cabins in the old Keesee tobacco factory lot on Front street. Dr. C. W. Beaumont, Health officer, went down to investigate the report and found it to be true. Measures were immediately taken by the Board of Health, assisted by the Board of Mayor and Aldermen to have the patient and all who were living in the house with him quarantined, until arrangements could be made to remove him from the city and take all precautionary measures to prevent the spread of the disease. Upon investigation it was found out that the case was clearly an imported one, the negro man whose name is Carter Russell, being a sort of peripatetic character, who wandered around from city to city, and had only returned here from Memphis or Cairo a few days previous. During the day a pest-house was secured about two miles from the city, out near the Paradise Hill road, in what was thought to be an isolated quarter, and the negro, together with his clothes, bedding, cooking utensils, provisions and a negro woman to nurse him, was carried out there.

The premises which he vacated were thoroughly disinfected, the other occupants of the house vaccinated and quarantined and all necessary measures taken to prevent the spread.

During the night, however, the house was visited by some unknown parties, the patient and negro woman ordered to leave, under pain of death if they refused, and the cabin burned to the ground. This is the tale the man and woman tell, though by many it is thought that they fired the house themselves, as the man was very loth to be carried away from town. However this may be, certian it is, the cabin was burned and the patient walked back to town that night and took up his abode in the same house from which he had been removed. Tuesday morning the authorities immediately set to work to find another place, far removed from any habitation, where the patient could be removed to and properly quarentined and cared for. It was found utterly impossible to secure a house, parties not only refused to rent one but threatened all kinds of violence to the patient and parties removing him if he was brought into their neighborhood.

It was under such disadvantages and discouragement as this that the Board of Health and Mayor and Aldermen worked, but they were equal to the emergency and soon procured tents and Tuesday night again had the patient removed from the city and placed in an isolated place (where, it is not necessary to say) far removed from any other abode.

To make the guarentine perfect and to insure the negro against violence or prevent his return to the city a guard heavily armed with shot gun and pistols has been set to watch the tent and it is safe to predict that no such disgraceful act as that perpetrated Monday night will be repeated.

The patient is attended by a competent physician and will receive every necessary attention.

At last reports, he was doing very well with every prospect of a final recovery.

And now, a word to all, and particularly our country friends. As before stated this is undoubtly an imported case of small-pox and there is no probability of its becoming an epidemic here. The proper authorities have taken every precautionary measure possible and express not the slightest fear that it will spread.

No other case has been reported during the entire week, and now that the warm days have come (small-pox is peculiarly a winter disease) you need feel no alarm, but if you want to come to the city you can do sh with perfect impunity and without the slightest risk. It may be well for all who have not yet been vaccinated to do so.

FLASHES FROM MACON.
Big Blaze in Cotton-A Citizen Buried in the Ruins-An Old Man Butchered by a Young Negress.
MACON, March 15 — A fire this morning, supposed to be accidental, broke out in the warehouse of C. D. Anderson & Son, on Fourth street. The flames soon enveloped the building and rapidly spread to the paper and rag warehouse of Wolff & Bro., and continued its work.

R. B. Watson, formerly a prominent cotton broker, is supposed to be buried beneath the debris, and his remains will be taken out to-morrow.

The total loss is $50,000, on which there was $21,500 insurance. Cotton was stored in the warehouse belonging to different parties, and nearly all of it was damaged. The firemen behaved splendidly.

At Summerfield, six miles from here, an old man named William A. Evans was foully murdered last night by Emma Johnson, colored, who used an axe to perpetrate the deed. Evans was in bed, and the blows were struck in the dark. The murderess was arrested and is now confined in jail.

She persistently denies any connection with the crime, but the evidence is conclusive. The murder was committed in Evans' store and for the sake of plunder. Emma is about sixteen years old, and seems perfectly indifferent.

At Summerfield the officers were surrounded by a mob of white and coated people, but by strenuous efforts lynching was prevented.

The experiment with the electric light at the Muscogee Mills on Monday worked to the satisfaction of all concerned. It is probable that the whole city of Columbus will be lighted up by electricity.

As the Southwestern Railroad passenger train ran on the Flint river bridge Monday afternoon a twelve-year-old tramp was found perched on the trucks under the passenger coach stealing a ride. The train was stopped and the youthful cosmopolitan rescued from his perilous position.

The case of the State vs. Carrie Massey, colored, charged with the murder of William Evans, in Summerfield, Bibb county, a short while ago, was marked for trial yesterday at Macon. The Telegraph and Messenger says that the case will be one of the most interesting of the term, as there is much more in it than has been given to the public.

Only two cases of small-pox developed in Atlanta during Sunday and Monday, although Sunday was very generally regarded by physicians as the last day of the period in which a fresh lot of cases might have reasonably been expected. The two cases were found Sunday and none were reported Monday. Thus it will be seen that the scare is about over, and that no cause for uneasiness any longer exists.

The wheat crop now being harvested in Jasper county is one of the very best ever produced there. There was a large area sown in fall oats, and they are about as good as the land, under any circumstances, could produce. The yield will be immense. Spring oats are not so good, but the recent rain will greatly improve the prospect.

The Butler Herald reports that Messrs. Peed & Halley have quite a curiosity at their store. Mr. J. L. Parker, while out in the woods a few days ago, discovered a fox den, in which were two young gray foxes, scarcely old enough to have their eyes opened. One of these animals Mr. Parker secured and brought to town, the other one having been carried away during his absence by the mother of the brutes. Messrs. Peed & Halley having a cat that had recently lost a brood of young kittens, the fox was given to her, and is now being nursed and raised by the cat with perfect care and devotion.

Three ladies and four gentlemen were baptised at Shallowford, about four miles from Gamesville, on Sunday.

Atlanta Post Appeal: "Two more victims are added to the pernicious influence of dime literature. Yesterday afternoon two little colored boys, Tommy Simonton and Aleck Wade, aged about twelve years, and living at M Vine street, while out for a Sunday stroll with a plum orchard in view, were sighted by a couple of white youths, alleged to be Walter Smith and Frank Wilson, going quietly down the road, who, taking them for bandits, probably Masters Smith and Wilson held a council of war, and Masters Smith, as it is alleged, fired upon the youthful colored pair, lodging a ball in the stomach of Tommy Simonton; firing again, the ball struck the left hand of young Wade. Much excitement was created in the vicinity of the tragedy, and it was not known who was responsible for the deed until the white infants mentioned were brought to the house, where they were recognized by the sufferers as the authors of their indisposition. The boys were arrested and lodged in the station house to await trial this afternoon."

Mowre Advertiser: "The other day the people of Forswyth were astonished to see four men march into town, bound and under the command of Mr James Krug. They kept up the line of march until they reached the jail. Their names are Sol Dillard, George Calhoun, Dave Hogan and Andy Taylor, and they are charged with burglary from the house of Mr John L. Ponder, who lives a few miles from Forswyth. For a long time—perhaps a year or more—Mr. Ponder has been missing articles from his house, his barn and smoke house, and he could not account for their disappearance. Finally he went into a long and patient investigation of the matter, and the result was the arrest of the four persons named. There is evidence that this party had been engaged in a system of combined pillage, and that they had keys to fit all the locks about Mr. Ponder's house—including the trunks, etc. A five-dollar bill was taken from Mrs. Ponder's trunk, which was all the time kept locked. Perhaps $20 in money have been stolen from the house, besides other things, the value of which cannot be estimated."

An equal number were then carried a short distance up the Oostanaula and deposited in that stream. These little fellows were only four days old when launched into the stream, though at that age appeared able to shift for themselves and take their chances with the big seventy five pounds cat fish which infest the rivers. VIRGINIA NEWS.
George C. Dulin had a valuable horse stolen from his stable at Springvale, Fairfax County, Monday night.
The chime bells on the steeple of Centennary Church, Richmond, were heard for the first time last Sunday.
Ex-Mayor Samuel A. Bailey, of Lynchburg, is lying dangerously ill at his residence on Diamond Hill, in that city.
Colonel A. S. Buford, of the Richmond and Danville road, is at Old Point Comfort, Fortress Monroe, in search of health.
The Ladies' Memorial Association of Portsmouth have set apart Friday, May 19, to be observed as Memorial Day for this year.
Mr. William A. Dennis, residing south of Leesburg, Loudoun County, died suddenly from neuralgia of the heart on Wednesday.
Mr. H. G. Peters, of Leavenworth, Henry County, has been awarded the orator's medal of the Washington Society of the University of Virginia.
Rev. Dr. John C. Granberry, of Lynchburg, is prominently spoken of as one of the coming Methodist bishops to be elected at Nashville May 5.
The remains of the late W. H. Wade, of the Baltimore Sun, which were recently buried in Shockoe Cemetery, Richmond, have been removed to Hollywood.
Mr. Alexander Johnson, an aged citizen of Loudoun County, died at his home, near Mount Gilead, Monday night last, in the seventy-seventh year of his age.
Mr. Samuel Campbell, for many years a resident of Loudoun County, died at the residence of his son-in-law, George A. Newman, in Louisville, Ky., April 19, in the eighty-fifth year of his age.
The residence of Robert Lindamood, at Bartonsville, Frederick County, was entirely destroyed by fire a few days ago. All the contents of the house were burned, the family not even saving a change of clothing.

Colonel Thomas Dodamead, who was at times the superintendent of the Chesapeake and Ohio, Richmond and Danville, Richmond and Petersburg, and Virginia and Tennessee Railroads, has removed to Richmond from South Carolina.

The Staunton Speciator learns that Erasmus Coffman, colored, a convict in the employ of Gooch & Mason, contractors on the Valley Railroad, about four miles south of Staunton, in attempting to escape last week, was shot twice by the guard and killed.

A man seventy-four years of age, named Clyne, stole a horse in Augusta County recently, sold the animal for $75 cash to a party near Montreal depot, and was arrested on the 14th at Mr. Edward Burks'. His excuse for committing the crime was the desire to obtain money with which to leave his wife.

The Lynchburg Virginian says: "The new caisson of the Richmond and Alleghany Railroad has been thoroughly tested by several trains, heavily loaded with passengers, being run through it. The work seems to be solid and substantial and the cars move smoothly and evenly on the rails."

A white man named Williams, a stonemason, residing near Massie's Mills, Nelson County, was seriously burned on Monday night. He was intoxicated, and fell down before a kiln for drying lumber. A colored man went to his assistance and found him in an unconscious state, with one of his legs burned to a crisp.

In Caroline County, last week, a colored boy, living on Mr. J. E. Dickinson's farm, became angry on account of something that did not please him at breakfast, and set fire to a stack of straw, by which a large barn, two stables, the corn-house, double servants' house, with brick chimneys, smoke-house, ice-house, dairy and another small building were consumed.

Captain McPhail, of the Richmond and Danville Railroad Company, has taken charge of the mineral bureau of the company, and is now preparing specimens of ores, &c., for exhibition in Richmond. The products and minerals of the territory tributary to that long line and its many branches will be fully shown up for the inspection of moneyed men and settlers.

Mr. R. ALBERTSON, 4207 Columbus avenue, Philadelphia, having received a severe contusion of the knee-cap, suffered intensely therefrom. A friend suggested St. Jacobs Oil, and before he had used three bottles he was a well man.

In the game of ball Monday between the Bowdoins and Tufts nine. College Hill, Massachusetts, the score stood: Bowdoins 7, Tufts 5.

At Malden, Mass., Sunday evening, Gerald Keegan, while returning home, had his throat badly cut by an unknown person, but the assailant fled, owing to Keegan's outcries. No arrests.

In North Providence yesterday E. W. Olney, a prominent citizen, was shot three times in the legs by John Kinnicutt. A quarrel about the sale of property was the cause. The balls have been extracted. Olney will recover.

The annual meeting of the Portland, Saco & Port mouth Railroad was held at Kittery depot Monday forenoon. The affairs of the road were reported to be in excellent condition. Elijah B. Phillips, Alfred P. Rockwell, William B. Bacon, Samuel C. Lawrence, George P. King. G. E. B. Jackson and Stephen J. Young were unanimously chosen directors.

The town of Epes, Sumpter county, Ala., was almost destroyed by fire Saturday night. The particulars are as follows: In the afternoon a crowd of drunken negroes became boisterous in the streets, insulting citizens and threatening violence. The white men banded together and drove the turbulent crowd out of town. After nightfall the negroes returned and set fire to the place. Seven stores were burned, but an estimate of losses and insurance cannot now be obtained. Four of the negroes implicated in the burning boarded the up train on the Alabama Great Southern Railroad, and were arrested when the train arrived here. They are now in jail and will be taken to Epes.

Men Found to Repiece Strikers.

CLEVELAND, June 5.—The Clevelandfl rolling-mills at Newburgh, started up this morning. About 500 men are at work. No violence has yet occurred, but trouble is brewing.

A Vessel Supposed to have Gone Down,

CHICAGO, June 4.—A South Haven special says that a board, bearing the name "Belle Richmond," came ashore there this evening, and it is feared that she has gone down with the crew.

Marine Disaster.

SOUTH HAVEN, Mich., June 4.—This evening the schooner "Industry," from St. Joseph, was capsized just north of this harbor. All on board were drowned.

Two Murdered Men.

MOOREHEAD, Minn., June 5.—The bodies of two murdered men, Mr. Washington and Fred. Fehrerback, were found in Redeey, 17 miles north of Perham, on Saturday. Washington was killed with buckshot and Fehrerback had his throat cut and a bullet wound in his left chest, and a wound from a club. Washington was a surveyor, and lived at Bay City, Michigan. Fehrerback lived near here. John Tibbet, aged 15, is suspected of the murders.

Another Disastrous Storm.

PETERSBURG, Va., June 4.—A storm this afternoon, extending from Halifax to Garrysburg, North Carolina, leveled houses, trees and fences. In the wreck of one house here two children were killed. Hailstones as large as a man's fist fell, damaging the crops seriously.

PARIS, June 4.—The Grand Prix de Paris for three-year-old colts and fillies, a mile and seven furlongs, was run today and won by Bruce, Fenelon second, Alhambra third. Keene's Romeo met with an accident this morning, and in consequence he did not run. The winner of the race is an English horse, and was ridden by Archer.

CHATTANOOGA, June 7.—A riot occurred Monday night between the whites and the blacks at Epps Station, in Sumter county, Alabama, in which the negroes were driven from town. They returned at midnight and set fire to the town, burning seven stores. Several negroes have been arrested, and others are being pursued. It is feared they will be lynched if captured.

FRED. W. NEWBURG, forger, who secured some $20,000 from the Ohio State Treasury and against whom fifty-two indictments were returned, has been taken to the Penitentiary for a term of six years, he having pleaded guilty to two indictments only.

Serious riots occurred Sunday between natives and Europeans, at Alexandria, Egypt. Several persons were killed and wounded, and a number of houses destroyed. The British Consul was dragged from his carriage and beaten, and the engineer of a British man of war was killed.

LIEUTENANT DANEHOWER has received a letter from Siberia which says that a memoradrum was found on DeLong's body, the last entry of which was made on October 18, nine days after Ninderman and Noros left. This entry states that four of the party were then dead and Collins was dying.

REV. MR. WATKINS, American Missionary in Jalisco, Mexico, was attacked by a mob, and taking refuge in his house, with a number of friends, made a spirited resistance, killing several. He afterwards surrendered. The Military Governor of the district has interposed in the prisoner's behalf.

NEAR Vienna, Ill., a bachelor, named J. W. Bayless, living alone, was found tied to a chair in his house, his feet burned to a crisp by a small lamp and his head split open with an ax. Some parties unknown evidently tortured him to make him tell the whereabouts of supposed money, but it is thought they found none.

The stern-wheel steamer Evansville, bound from Evansville to Bowling Green, Ky., collapsed a flue near Calhoun, Ky., on Green River. Two of her crew were killed and ten others injured by the disaster. The Evansville belonged to the Green and Barren River Navigation Company, and was in her second season.

ARMISTED GRAY, colored, was hanged Friday, June 9, at Powhatan Court House, Va. Quirino Gaitan was hanged at Brownsville, Texas. An Indian murderer was hanged in Indian Territory. John Tribbett, seventeen years of age, who murdered two persons a few days ago, was hanged by a mob at Perham, Minnesota.

The Sheriff has captured at Kirwin, Kansas, two counterfeiters, set of dies and unfinished coins. The prisoners hint strongly of their connection with gangs operating from St. Louis, Chicago and New York. Many Kansas towns have been systematically worked for the past six months. Thousands of small counterfeit coins are in circulation.

The President has nominated the following for members of the Tariff Commission: Wm. A. Wheeler, of New York, Chairman; John L. Hayes, of Massachusetts; Henry W. Oliver, Jr., of Pennsylvania; Austin M. Garland, of Illinois; Jacob Ambler, of Ohio; John S. Phelps, of Missouri; Robert P. Porter, District of Columbia; John W. H. Underwood, of Georgia; Duncan F. Kenner, of Louisiana.

Mr. E. P. B. Brown, originally the manager and subsequently the proprietor of the Aikens Newspaper Union Establishment, Cincinnati, has disposed of that concern to the A. N. Kelogg Newspaper Company. The employes of the Union attested their appreciation of Mr. Brown by presenting him with an elegant gold-headed ebony cane, and he responded by giving them a banquet. Mr. Brown retires to his model farm, at Liberty, Ind.

News from Decatur, Alabama, states that a riot took place a few nights since between colored men and whites at Epes Station, Sumter County. The whites drove the negroes from the town. The latter returned at midnight, set fire to the town, and seven stores were burned. Four negroes have been arrested and others are being pursued. There are fears of lynching, as the respectable negroes are very much inensed, and would not interfere if the whites took such a step.

Doyle, convicted in Chicago of having in his possession counterfeit bonds, offers through counsel to prove conclusively the genuineness of the $1,000 bond plate, how it was obtained and all about it, provided the Government will release him from confinement. Secretary Folger and other Treasury officials deny, in the most positive terms, that there are any spurious bonds in circulation, on the ground that, if any were in circulation, they certainly would have known something about it before now.

Twenty-one infantry and seven artillery companies have been entered for the free for all prizes at the July encampment, at Indianapolis. Among the infantry companies are the Born Zouaves, St. Louis; Folger Corps, Geneva; Luckey Zouaves, Chicago; Crescent Rifles, New Orleans; Porter Rifles, Nashville.

The Ohio Republican State Convention was held at Columbus, Ohio, June 7. General R. P. Kennedy, of Logan County, presided. For Secretary of State, Hon. Charles Townsend, present incumbent, and for Judge of the Supreme Court, John H. Doyle, of Toledo, were nominated by acclamation. C. A. Flickinger, of Defiance, was nominated for member of the Board of Public Works. The platform indores the administration of President Arthur and Governor Foster, condemns the persecution of the Jews in Europe, indores protection of American industry, declares that the traffic in liquor should pay its share of the State taxes, and that laws upon the statute books must be respected until repealed or abrogated.

When news of Bourke's murder reached London his brother went into the lobby of the Commons and accused Parnell and Biggar with being the cause thereof. On Saturday night last some party or parties fired the corn crib of Mr. J. L. Hall, in Laurens county, and discharged a pistol to attract the attention of the family. The inmates of the house rushed out, and in their absence the dwelling was entered and robbed of a trunk containing money and valuable papers. The trunk was found later broken open. Four negroes have been arresed on suspicion.

One of the machines for the electric light company has arrived at Columbus. The company will begin operations as soon as the full complement of machinery is received.

A company is now being organized at Athens to start a laboratory for the wholesale manufacture of drugists' chemicals of all kinds.

Love Wilder, express messenger between Albany and Smithville, met with quite a serious accident Tuesday. He was dismounting from the express wagon from the rear, when his foot caught in some way, and he was thrown violently against the edge of the depot platform upon his stomach.

J. H. Garner arrested Jack Jones, colored, in Newman last Tuesday, upon the charge of murder, it being supposed that he is the individual who shot Chandler Arnold on the night of the 38th of December, ult., and for whose arrest and conviction the Governor offered a reward of $150.

The Ciceronian and Phi Delta societies of Mercer University have sent a challenge to the Demosthenian and Phi Kappa, of the Georgia University, to meet them in debate, in Macon, on the 38th of June next, during Mercer commencement. The challenge has been accepted, and a few days since the Demosthenian and Phi Kappa societies met and selected their representatives. These are Messrs. P. H. Bell, of Atlanta; H. V. Washington, of Macon; and H. H. Phinizy, of Athens. The Mercer representatives have not yet been selected, nor has the subject of debate been chosen.

Mr. R. T. Bean, a married man, and Mrs. Ariminta Thompson, a married woman, both of Newnan, left their families Tuesday morning and tied the town on an elopement tour. They went to Atlanta together, but soon after their arrival the Sheriff of Coweta county put in an appearance in search of the couple. With the aid of Atlanta officers not much time was wasted in finding the parties, and they were promptly arrested. The man and woman were handcuffed and locked together, and in this condition carried back to Newnan under the surveillance of the Sheriff.

It is thought that two white tramps burned the house of Floyd King, in Oconee, a few nights ago, as they were seen hanging around the neighborhood, and two tracks were found around the building next morning. King is an industrious colored man, who accumulated some $5,000 since the war.

One day last week a little child of Thomas Gunter, who lives on R. B. Mathew's place in Oglethorpe, was missed, and search being instituted, it was soon found in a tub of water with life, to all appearances, extinct. After hard work, however, it was brought to, and has entirely recovered.

Athens Watchman: "A Northern company (supposed to be the Inman) last Saturday closed a trade for the Barnett Snooks property. They paid $22,500 for the Oconee side, including a half mile of fall and 60) acres of land, and $100 for Mrs. Tinsdal's property opposite, with 70 acres. At the July term of Oconee Court a charter will be granted and work will commence at once. They will spend $750,000 preparing the land for manufactories."

KILLED AT CHARLESTON.
A Negro Barber Ruthlessly Shoots Down a White Man and Escapes.
Special Dispatch to the Intelligencer.
CHARLESTON, W. VA., May 2.—About 12 o'clock, last night, a negro, named Haston Whiting, shot dead T. S. Greaves, a white man, in front of Markley's saloon. It appears that the negro asked the white man to drink with him and was refused, whereupon the negro stepped out on the pavement and shot Greaves, as he came out, the bullet taking effect in the left breast, one inch to the right of the nipple, causing death in twenty minutes. The negro is at large and officers are after him.

Threats are uttered of dire vengeance, if the murderer is caught. Whiting is a mulatto, a barber, twenty-five years old; he came here from Gallapolis, Ohio, his home, two months ago, having left that place for dangerously cutting a negro woman. Greaves was a plasterer and leaves a wife and children, living in Huntington, West Virginia. Two hundred dollars' reward is offered for the arrest of the negro. Detective Burnett and the force are after him.

Just as the city began to quiet down Monday night, after the busy scenes incident upon "show day," the cry of murder startled the few stragglers yet upon our streets, the particulars of which we lay before our readers today.—Samuel Greaver, the murdered man, with some friends, dropped into John Marley's saloon on Kanawha street, near 12 o'clock Monday night, and were enjoying a glass of beer in the back' room, when Houston Whiting, a colored barber employed by Bullard & Robinson, also came into the saloon. He invited one of the gentlemen friends of Mr. Greaver to the bar to take a glass of beer. While they were drinking, some other gentlemen came in, one of whom Whiting began to abuse, and displaying a revolver, swore he was going to shoot some d—n white man. His friends, among whom were two other colored men of this city, tried to offend him down, and Mr. White, a brick layer employed on the Capitol, caught hold of him and pushed him out of the door. As he did so, the negro drew his revolver and aimed it at Mr. Bert Ong, a white man against whom he had a grudge; a colored man jerked Mr. Ong to one slur; as he did so, Mr. Greaver, who was a stranger and had not spoken to the negro, was advancing from the rear room toward the door, as it to pass out, the murderous villain then leveled his revolver at him and fired, the ball taking effect in the upper part of his left lung, causing death by internal hemorrhage. The victim of the rash act turned, reeled to the rear room, where he fell to the floor, exclaiming "I am shot," and expired in thirty minutes. The murderer then fled. Dr. Wagner was immediately called, the authorities were notified, but the life of the innocent, unoffending stranger had gone out. Three Negro Murderers Hanged from a Bridge in View of a Train Full of People.
Three Negro Murderers Hanged from a Bridge in View of a Train Full of People.

LAWRENCE, KANSAS, June 11.—A few days ago David Bausman of Ohio came to Lawrence to meet a brother. Not finding him he indulged too freely in liquor and on June 3 was found dead in the river. The Vinegar family were at once suspected. In the course of a day or two proof of their guilt was obtained, and Peter Vinegar, George Robinson, Ike King, and Sis Vinegar, all negroes, were arrested. From confessions made it appeared that Sis, a girl of 16 years, planned the murder. She enticed Bausman to meet her at a secluded point upon the river. Here King and Robinson were concealed and despatched their victim with a hammer and club despite his piteous appeals. Sis meanwhile urging them to spare his life as she had gotten his money. The fastening of this crime on the Vinegar gang led to the belief that they were responsible for many other murders committed near here under circumstances recalling the crimes of the Bender family, a woman always luring the victim to death.

Early yesterday morning a large armed mob broke into the jail and secured Vinegar, Robinson, and King. A ballot was then taken to decide whether Sis Vinegar should also be trken, which resulted in a tie vote. An additional vote against taking her was cast at another ballot, and she was left in the jail. Vinegar and King were stolid, and had little to say, but Robinson broke down and dropped on his knees several times, begging for his life. They were taken to the iron wagon bridge over the Kansas river, a distance of about a square from the jail. The arms of the prisoners had been pinioned and the ropes adjusted about their necks before leaving the jail. Upon reaching the middle span of the bridge Robinson's rope was secured to the iron work of the bridge. A dozen strong arms lifted him from his feet and dropped him over, but in doing so the rope binding his arms became unfastened, and reaching up he caught hold of the rope which was about his neck, and tried to save himself, making his death slow and painful. Vinegar followed, and died without a struggle. King's death was also speedy.

During the progress of the execution, the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe midnight passenger train, which passed under the bridge at the south end, came in, and passengers alighting for Lawrence were held by the mob until the job was finished. The bodies were cut down at about 7 o'clock this morning and placed in the jail yard. Threats were heard among the colored men of North Lawrence against the leaders of the mob, but there seems little prospect of further trouble.

Sr. Louis, Mo., June 11.—The lynching of the three negroes, Vinegard, Robinson and King at Lawrence, Kan., early Saturday morning was because, from their own confession and testimony given at the examination, it was conclusively shown they were the murderers of David Bausman, whose dead body was found in the Kansas River ten days ago. The circumstances which led to this action by Judge Lynch are as follows: Less than ten days since David Bausman, a well-to-do farmer from southern Ohio, reached Lawrence on a visit to some relatives who reside in the county, and getting to town after dark he concluded to remain all night before going to his brother's house. The men were not given time even for a prayer, although King begged for a few moments in which to prepare himself, and upon the arrival of the mob at the river bank the three murderers were pushed from the eastern pier of the bridge, one end of the ropes having been attached to the stringers. When it became known about Lawrence during the early hours this morning that the men had been lynched the greatest excitement prevailed. The State University is located at that point and the city is overcrowded with visitors from abroad, the commencement exercises being at their height. On every side deep regret is uttered that the town has been so disgraced; but not a word of sympathy is uttered for the murderers. It is known that the lynching party came from the eastern portion of Douglas county, near where the murdered man's relatives resided, but they also had the assistance and co operation of many citizens. Not since that August day in 1863 when the rebel guerilla Quantrell rode into Lawrence and sacked the city with his horde of Missouri cutthroats, leaving the dead bodies of eighty citizens behind, has the city passed through such a state of excitement as during the past twenty-four hours.

Bausman came to Lawrence in the latter part of May, to be near two brothers who lived in Douglass county. He had sold a farm in Ohio for a goodly sum and was supposed to have the money with him. He had displayed his roll of greenbacks in the presence of some negroes, which excited their cupidity and led to the plan to murder him.

With this end in view a daughter of Peter Vinegar, a woman of bad character, was employed to entice the victim to the vicinity of an ice house on the Kansas river. Here he was approached from behind and hit with a hammer by King and his head was pounded in with a club by Robertson. They then threw the body in the river and intimidated two boys who saw the affair. The girl seized the man's pocket book and took it to her father.

Robertson and King fled the town. The next day the body was found in the river, and the boys told their story. Vinegar and his daughter were arrested at once. Robertson was captured the following day at Independence, Mo., and Monday night King was caught near Eudora and taken to Lawrence. On Friday the examination of the murderers was held, and the woman, King and Robertson all confessed. There was much talk of lynching, and excitement ran high and finally culminated early Saturday morning by the hanging of the three men.

The Lawrence Journal, of Saturday, gives the following account of the affair:

At 1 o'clock last night fifty or more men made their appearance at the jail, and demanded admittance. Sheriff Asher refused, and to the best of his ability defended the property of the county. The lynching party had come armed with sledge hammers and cold chisels, and cut their way through every barrier. A Journal reporter, who was so unfortunate as to be on the street, was shut in and could not get out. Deputy Sheriff Estes coming to the jail from town, found himself an outsider. Estes has charge of the keys, and when he found that either the jail would tumble or admission be granted, he said: "Let me come in." There was no come in, but the Journal man was made a go-between to see what was wanted. Estes said the keys were at his house and if it was the determination to tear down the jail he would rather they should have the keys. The Journal man was told to go for those keys, and he went like a little man, but when he got back the last lock had been cut and the mob had the prisoners. They were marched to the bridge, and on the middle pier a halt was made. Prayers were short then. Pete Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaat King were each swung over the bridge and their bodies left dangling over the muddy Kaw. A crowd tried to get down to the scene of the hanging but so perfect was the arrangement of the vigilance committee that not a man, friend or foe, could get near. As the vigilants came back this crowd cheered them lustily. Most of the men were masked, though a few were simply blacked. It was asserted by those present that two-thirds of the Lawrence lynching party were black men.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and like King were taken from jail Saturday morning at 1 o'clock by a crowd of vigilants and hanged from the bridge. Sheriff Asher offered all the resistance in his power, but was compelled to submit. Robertson plead for his life and fell on his knees three times while being taken from jail to the point of execution. King said when he was to drop, "Boys, let me down easy." The men behind said: "Did you let Bausman down easy," and give King a snove. The necks of Vinegar and Robertson were broken; that of King was not. Vinegar who was considered almost worthless had his life insured for $5,000.

The general impression in Lawrence seems to be that the lynchers came from the neighborhood in which the Bausman brothers live, although there was a certain willingness on the part of Lawrence people.

While the deed is depreciated by the good citizens of Lawrence, they feel thankful that three at least of the Lawrence roughs will make honest life unpleasant no more.

THE LAWRENCE LYNCHING.
The recent lynching at Lawrence deserves more than a passing notice. The growing frequency of such scenes throughout the country is an alarming symptom; and that such a thing should be tolerated at Lawrence, "the city of schools and churches, and the seat of our great University," makes one feel as if the foundations were indeed giving way.

The facts of the case are fresh in the public mind. The body of a murdered man was found in the river. Following up certain indications, the two men who committed the murder were captured and lodged in jail. The police also arrested two notorious characters, Pete and Sister Vinegar as accomplices.

About midnight on Friday, June 9, a company of masked men went to the jail, demanded admission and secured it, took out the three men and hung them to the bridge. The men were sure of conviction and sure of punishment, and there was not a shadow of excuse for the lynching beyond what exists in every case of murder. It was a high-handed outrage which deserved the severest condemnation of every law-loving citizen.

It is sometimes asked: "If these men deserved their punishment, what does it matter whether they received it at the hands of a mob or at the hands of the court?" Society has adopted a method of ascertaining and punishing guilt. The mob method is a return to the ways of the lowest barbarism. In this case the guilt was clear. But a maddened mob never inquires closely as to evidence. Suspicion is just as good as proof when a mob once starts. A few months since there was a most brutal, unprovoked murder committed in Emporia. It excited intense indignation, and there was a plot to lynch the murderer. The officers, however, managed to foil the lynchers. At the examination it was ascertained beyond a question that the man was insane, and he was sent to the asylum. Had the mob caught him, they would have torn in pieces a poor lunatic. "Little loss," you say. Perhaps so, as far as the man was concerned, but his slayers would be bloody men to the day of their death.

In Kansas city a short time since, a foul crime was committed and a man arrested for it. The mob took the man arrested and dragged him through the streets, jumped on him; kicked him, and finally killed him amid a scene of howling disorder which would have disgraced a troop of caunibals. If the wildest Indian tribe should be as brutal to a prisoner, there would be a general demand for their extermination. After all was done, it was found that the man was innocent. The wrong man had been killed. But then the mob never stops for such trifles as this. They had their sport, they had gratified their thirst for blood, and somebody had been killed, they cared little who it might be.

There is nothing so blind and brutal as a mob. The law is slow and sometimes makes mistakes, but the most poorly executed laws are infinitely better and safer than the rule of a mob of midnight madmen. At Lawrence they are fearing retaliation from the colored people. It is not strange they should. They who sow the wind very naturally expect the whirlwind.

It is hinted that "some of the best people of Lawrence were in this." We cannot believe it. If there were any such people concerned in it, we are sorry for them. We should think they would want to wear their masks continually to hide the shame of their faces. We will guarantee them one thing; they will remember that "bridge at midnight" to the last and longest day of their life, and the howling of the midnight wind will mean more to them in the future than ever in the past.

The notorious Sis Vinegar was convicted of murder in the second degree for her complicity in the murder of David Bausman, at Lawrence, Kas., last May. Sis Vinegar, who is a negro prostitute, lured Bausman, a well-to-do farmer to a lonely spot on the river bank, where he was robbed and murdered by Ike King and George Robertson, accomplices of Sis, and his body thrown into the river. The murder was witnessed by four children, who made known the perpetrators, and although they had both fled they were captured and a week afterward, with Pete Vinegar, Sis' father, were taken from the jail by a mob and hung from the bridge.

The people in the towns of Sabetha and Netawaka, Kan., have been complaining for some time bitterly of the irregularity of their mails and losses which frequently occurred. Inspector John M. Crowell of the postoffice department began investigating matters, and effected the arrest of one, Chas. Smith, the mail carrier between the points named. He confesses to having opened for many weeks, almost every letter that came into his possession in any manner. He is bound over in the United States courts under bond for proper appearance.

The Alta Arizona contains the following account by Judge J. E. Stevens of a terrible shooting affair at Hackberry, A. T., on Feb. 20: Joseph Welden came into Hackberry about 10 A. M. He hired an Indian to hold his mule in an available place for a quick exit from town. His first recorded exploit was to try and get his work in on Edward Powers, who, thinking discretion the better part of valor, made good time out of range. His next demonstration was to order Bailey, the saloon-keeper, to hold up his hands, while Joe held his revolver at his head, cocked. This style of amusement lasted about an hour, when Dr. Day came into the saloon and invited Joe to drink. After the drinks, the Doctor attempted to put his hand in his pocket for money to pay, when Joe ordered him to hold up his hands, which the Doctor promptly did, at the same time sidling towards the door, through which he passed just as a bullet from Joe's pistol struck the casing on the left side of the door. Some half an hour later Day and John Bullock entered the saloon, when the Doctor said: "Joe, take a drink with us." Joe took his liquor in his left hand, holding his cocked pistol in his right, backed into the corner of the room and drank; returned and placed the glass on the counter, leaned against the counter with his pistol in his right hand laid across the counter, his left arm resting on it. In this position Joe ordered Bullock to approach him, which he did, when Joe said, "You have a pistol?" Bullock said "Yes," and with his left hand pulled a small five-shooter from his left coat pocket, changed it to his right hand and cocked it, holding it pointed towards Joe, who had his pistol against Bullock's breast. The next known occurrence was a discharge of Welden's pistol, followed by the retreat of Bullock, doubled up by the shot, and pursued by Joe with his pistol close to his back, into which he discharged two shots so close as to set fire to his clothing. Charley Spencer called on Joe to cease firing and surrender. Joe sent a shot so close to Charley as to graze his neck and ran toward his mule, when fire was opened upon him by citizens, and a shot struck him which brought him down.

LYNCHED BY A MOB

Enfuriated Men in Kansas City

String a Man Up.

National Associated Press.

KANSAS CITY, April 3.—Officer Pat Jones, of the Metropolitan police force of this city, was shot this evening by a colored man whose name is unknown. The policeman had just arrived at his home after his day's duty, when a proprietor of a grocery store pointed out to him two colored men who were carrying away some articles supposed to have been stolen from a freight car.

Jones at once started in pursuit of the alleged thieves, and when he came close to them one of them turned and fired three shots, one of which struck the policeman in the region of the heart, killing him instantly. A colored man was arrested on suspicion, and while a squad of policemen were taking him to the station house, a mob made a desperate attack on them. The police, with drawn weapons and by a determined fight, succeeded in taking their prisoner to the jail.

A colored man, name unknown, was afterwards taken by the desperate mob and hung from a bridge in the heart of the city. There is considerable excitement over the affair, people generally believing the lynched man was innocent of the crime charged against him.

The mob, however, neglected to tie the man's hands behind his back, and by holding the rope about his neck with both hands for six hours, he succeeded in saving his life, and was cut down the next day by friends. The poor fellow cannot tell who the parties were who committed this outrage, nor how many there were in the gang. He only knows that he went through the horrors of death, and is still bruised about his face and neck. He was brought to this city, and is now out on the Alazen creek, near town, with friends.
